name: McCarthy v. Madigan
event: The Court reviews dismissal of a federal prisoner’s damages-only constitutional medical-care action for failure to complete the Bureau of Prisons’ general grievance process.
questions: Whether Congress requires this exhaustion and, if not, whether the particular grievance procedure’s purposes and practical effects justify making it a prerequisite to this damages action.
baseline: All February 25–26 decisions and the committed March 3 Willy decision are effective. None changes statutory exhaustion or the established medical-care damages channel; the relevant public-law refresh preceded final assembly.
record: McCarthy alleges deliberate indifference by four Leavenworth prison employees to needs following a back operation and psychiatric problems. He expressly requests only money damages. The district court dismissed for nonexhaustion and denied reconsideration; the Tenth Circuit affirmed on the usefulness of administrative consideration and fact development even without damages authority. The general BOP regulations provide investigation and written responses but no hearing, formal evidentiary findings or monetary award. They require an initial complaint within 15 days, then appeals within 20 and 30 days, with extensions for valid reasons. An earlier grievance concerned a private cell; a later medical grievance was accepted despite lateness and denied by the warden, but its regional appeal was rejected as late. That sequence does not establish misconduct by grievance officials. McCarthy seeks reversal and ordinary damages litigation; respondents invoke agency autonomy, information, general statutory delegation, §1997e, possible FTCA conversion and settlement.
entering: Patsy v. Board of Regents of Florida, 457 U.S. 496; McKart v. United States, 395 U.S. 185; McGee v. United States, 402 U.S. 479; and Coit Independence Joint Venture v. FSLIC, 489 U.S. 561, require attention to statutory design and the practical purposes of exhaustion. The contemporaneous 42 U.S.C. §1997e addresses specified state-prisoner §1983 actions through limited discretionary stays; it does not govern this federal Bivens action. General BOP authority under 18 U.S.C. §4042 does not expressly mandate exhaustion. Regulations 28 C.F.R. part 542 (1991) govern the described grievance procedure; FTCA claims have a different process under part 543. Carlson v. Green, 446 U.S. 14, supplies an existing constitutional medical-care damages channel; Bush v. Lucas, 462 U.S. 367, and Schweiker v. Chilicky, 487 U.S. 412, address distinct comprehensive congressional schemes. Hudson’s force holding creates no exhaustion rule, and Willy’s collateral Rules authority does not create one either. Later statutes and later restrictions on constitutional remedies are excluded.
reach: Only the exhaustion ground preventing adjudication is decided. The existing Carlson setting is accepted without creating a new constitutional cause. The allegations are not findings of deliberate indifference; liability, immunity, causation and amount remain for ordinary proceedings. Prospective relief and materially different administrative schemes are outside the question.
stoneCheck: The effective prior decisions leave the approved statute-first, purpose-sensitive analysis intact. Stone joins the absence-of-mandate determination and the specific balance of unavailable compensation, deadlines and limited adjudicative benefit. His join does not excuse an express statutory condition or extend Bivens. No new damages, merits element or unpresented defense is resolved.
action: The Tenth Circuit’s exhaustion judgment is reversed, 9–0, and the case is remanded for ordinary proceedings on the damages complaint.

components.title: Dismissal for failure to exhaust the general BOP grievance procedure
components.remedy: The damages-only action may proceed without completion of this process; no liability or damages award is made.

holdings.title: Statutory design governs the exhaustion inquiry
holdings.rule: An express congressional exhaustion requirement controls according to its terms. Where Congress has not required exhaustion, courts must exercise sound discretion consistent with the statutory scheme, weighing prompt access to court against the actual interests in agency authority and judicial efficiency; neither the general BOP delegation nor the then-current §1997e imposes a mandatory gate for this federal prisoner’s Bivens medical-care claim.
holdings.authority: Blackmun’s opinion, joined by Stone, White, Stevens, O’Connor, Kennedy and Souter; seven Justices control the governing inquiry and statutory application.
holdings.explanation: The Court holds that a judicial exhaustion rule must fit Congress’s design and the purposes served by the actual administrative process. Patsy makes congressional intent central, while McKart and McGee explain why administrative expertise, correction of error and useful fact development matter when courts retain discretion. Coit distinguishes that discretion from a statutory command. Congress’s general assignment of prison administration to the Bureau says nothing requiring this prisoner to exhaust before seeking damages. Section 1997e’s limited treatment of certain state-prisoner actions does not enact a broader federal rule by implication. Carlson supplies the established medical-care damages channel; Bush and Schweiker concern comprehensive remedial choices Congress made in different programs. The Bureau’s own grievance procedure is not an equivalent congressional substitute. Respondents’ appeal to administrative autonomy therefore requires examination of what this procedure can accomplish, rather than automatic dismissal. The Court does not displace an express statutory requirement, announce a new Bivens action or determine the medical claim’s merits.
precedents: *Patsy v. Board of Regents of Florida*, 457 U.S. 496 — applied for congressional primacy and the actual limited scope of contemporaneous §1997e.
*McKart v. United States*, 395 U.S. 185 — applied for the purposes of agency authority, expertise, correction and efficiency.
*McGee v. United States*, 402 U.S. 479 — applied for sound judicial discretion where Congress has not clearly required exhaustion.
*Coit Independence Joint Venture v. FSLIC*, 489 U.S. 561 — applied to distinguish statutory exhaustion and the adequacy of an administrative route.
*Carlson v. Green*, 446 U.S. 14 — preserved as the existing medical-care damages channel, without extending it to a new context.
*Bush v. Lucas*, 462 U.S. 367 — distinguished: no comparable comprehensive congressional remedial scheme displaces this existing channel.
*Schweiker v. Chilicky*, 487 U.S. 412 — distinguished on the same absence of a congressional replacement scheme.

holdings.title: This damages-only claim need not pass through the general BOP process
holdings.rule: Absent a statutory mandate, a federal prisoner seeking only damages for the completed medical-care wrong alleged here need not exhaust the described BOP process: it cannot award compensation, its short filing periods risk forfeiture, and its limited adjudicative benefit does not outweigh access to court. The result does not decide a request for prospective relief, a procedure able to grant the sought compensation, or a materially different administrative adjudication.
holdings.authority: The same seven Justices join Blackmun’s particular balancing and application. Scalia and Thomas agree with the result solely because no money remedy is available; their judgment concurrence does not join the deadline or broader balancing rationale.
holdings.explanation: The Court holds that this grievance process provides too little countervailing benefit to justify barring the damages complaint. McKart requires attention to the process’s real function, not merely its administrative label. Investigation and written responses may help officials improve care, but they neither compensate this completed injury nor create formal findings on which a court can conclusively dispose of the claim. The successive filing periods also risk forfeiture; extensions exist, but their valid-reason condition does not remove that practical burden, illustrated by the rejected regional appeal. Coit’s concern for an adequate route and Turner’s protection of valid prisoner claims inform the balance. The proposed conversion to an FTCA claim and possible settlement do not establish an effective damages remedy in these regulations or this record; Hillsborough cautions against requiring an uncertain route to relief. Ordinary litigation remains available for developing facts and asserting defenses. The Court decides no medical violation, improper grievance handling or exhaustion rule for prospective relief.
precedents: *McKart v. United States*, 395 U.S. 185 — applied through a claim-specific comparison of individual and institutional interests.
*Coit Independence Joint Venture v. FSLIC*, 489 U.S. 561 — its adequacy principle informs the practical evaluation; the filing-period application is not a categorical invalidation of short deadlines.
*Turner v. Safley*, 482 U.S. 78 — applied for continued judicial cognizance of valid prisoners’ constitutional claims, without deciding this claim’s validity.
*Hillsborough Township v. Cromwell*, 326 U.S. 620 — applied against forcing resort to an uncertain administrative avenue for the requested relief.
*Union Pacific Railroad Co. v. Board of County Commissioners*, 247 U.S. 282 — applied for the significance of uncertainty in the available administrative remedy.

nonholding: No general exception to a congressional exhaustion command is created. Prospective relief, an administrative monetary remedy and materially different adjudicative procedures remain open. The Court makes no finding of bias, deliberate indifference, damages entitlement or loss of a defense. It does not transform negligence into a constitutional violation or extend Bivens to a new context.
law: Effective March 4, courts may not dismiss this damages-only federal medical-care action for failure to complete the described general BOP grievance process. Seven Justices apply the statute-first and purpose-sensitive inquiry, including the deadline burden and limited factual record; the two judgment concurrences share only the narrower no-compensation ground. Congress’s express requirements retain their own force, and Carlson’s established channel is preserved without expansion. Future procedures and prospective claims remain distinct.
separate: Scalia, joined by Thomas, agrees with reversal solely because the Bureau’s process offers no monetary relief to a claimant seeking only damages. McNeese v. Board of Education, 373 U.S. 668, and Montana National Bank v. Yellowstone County, 276 U.S. 499, support that effective-remedy ground. They withhold the broader general-exhaustion discussion and its unmodified application to Bivens, and reject treating these reasonable filing periods, with extensions, as a reason to excuse exhaustion.
continuity: Scalia and Thomas, concurrence in judgment, March 4: absence of monetary relief alone defeats exhaustion of this damages-only grievance; McNeese and Montana National Bank supply the adequate-remedy principle. They do not join the broader framework’s unmodified use for Bivens and reject reliance on reasonable filing deadlines with extensions. The no-compensation ground is shared with the Court; the contrary deadline and methodology positions are noncontrolling. No later treatment.
procedure: Supreme Court review ends with reversal and remand. The federal damages complaint may proceed without exhaustion of this general grievance process, subject to ordinary adjudication and defenses. No damages amount, deliberate-indifference finding, immunity decision or retained Supreme Court supervision is entered.
dependencies: Later prisoner cases must use the then-effective statute and actual remedy/claim, preserve the distinction between force and medical care, and identify any changed administrative process. The general grievance regulations do not silently import FTCA exhaustion or confer authority to pay damages.
formBasis: the unanimous disposition rests on a seven-Justice Court rationale and a two-Justice narrower concurrence; Stone’s approved reasoning changes the controlling coalition relative to history.
sourceMap: 503 U.S. 141–144 verifies the complaint, regulations, filing periods, grievance sequence and lower judgment; pages 144–156 verify statutory design, competing purposes, actual remedy limits and reservations; pages 156–158 verify the narrower concurrence. The grievance chronology is drawn from the official account of the briefs and argument, not from an independently reviewed transcript.

audit.provisional: Reverse under Patsy/McKart’s statutory and practical analysis: Congress imposes no mandate here, the Bureau cannot compensate, the deadlines risk forfeiture and the process lacks a formal evidentiary record. Carlson supplies the existing channel; decide no merits or defense.
audit.reconciliation: Historical judgment and sufficient ground match; no material revision or non-Stone historical departure.

alternatives: A congressional-mandate route fails because neither §4042 nor the actual §1997e applies such a command. Comprehensive-scheme displacement fails because Carlson’s existing setting is not replaced by a congressional alternative. Administrative investigation is useful but does not resolve the only requested relief or create binding evidentiary findings. FTCA conversion and settlement cannot be assumed from speculative authority or practice. The narrower no-money-remedy route independently supports Scalia and Thomas’s result, but does not make them join the majority’s reliance on deadlines.
auditFinal: Nine reverse and remand; seven join the stated statutory inquiry and particular balance, while Scalia and Thomas concur only on the remedy mismatch. Stone’s supported join changes the majority coalition without moving any non-Stone vote or ground. No unapproved exception to statutory exhaustion, prospective claim disposition or new Bivens context enters the holding.
